title: Navigation for an independent school
metaTitle: Navigation for an independent school site
excerpt: The menu should list parent jobs: the day, a visit, fees, and ages. One header path should visit or inquire. Department names can stay off it.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper, a map of jobs rather than a map of departments.
caption: The sketch is labeled with goals. A school menu should be labeled that way too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a school menu say?
faqs.answer: The day, visit, fees, ages, and a way to ask what a date cannot hold. Use year names families already say. Flourish, journey, and advancement are internal or ceremonial. They do not help a parent find a fee on a Sunday night.

faqs.question: Where does the visit link go?
faqs.answer: To dates or to a short inquiry, in the header, on every page. If many families cannot tour yet, the label can say visit or inquire, as long as the page splits those paths immediately. Do not land the tap on a history and a PDF.

faqs.question: What belongs in the footer instead?
faqs.answer: Policies, the phone number, the door, privacy, and news if you publish it. Current-parent business, such as a parents' association, can sit there too. The header stays stable. Mark the current page so three open tabs do not blur together.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Independent school website navigation should be a map of the jobs a parent arrives with, not a map of your departments. For someone deciding where a child will spend years, the labels should be words they already use, and one path should visit or inquire. If a label only makes sense in a staff meeting, it is in the wrong menu.

WCAG groups its requirements under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A menu has to be operable and understandable. People must find it, use it without guessing, and predict where a label lands. That includes phones. A handsome menu that fails those tests still fails, even when the crest is perfectly spaced.

## The jobs they arrive with

Most parents land with one of five jobs. See the day their child would have. Find out when they can visit. Understand the fees. Learn the ages you teach and whether a year is open. Ask a question the visit page cannot hold, often about support or a move from another city. The navigation should finish those jobs in a label or two.

Write the jobs on paper before you name the labels. Then point each job at a real URL. The day. Visit. Fees. Ages. A question. If two jobs share a page, the label should be the job they will recognize, and the page should contain both. Do not point "Fees" at a homepage that hopes they will scroll past a motto.

Some parents arrive from a map pin with a narrower job: confirm this is the school on this street, and find the door for a visit they already booked. "Find the gate" earns a label when the entrance is easy to miss. It does not earn a label when the page is only an embedded map and a Latin line.

Ignore jobs that are yours. Updating a newsletter. Thanking donors. Recruiting a teacher. Those can live in the footer if they must exist. They are not the menu a parent needs on a Sunday night while a child is asleep and the decision is loud.

## Labels they already use

Use The day, Visit, Fees, Ages, and the name of the school. Use the year names families say. If learning support decides applications, "Learning support" is a clearer label than "Pastoral," because the parent is not browsing a care philosophy. They are asking whether you can meet a specific child.

Reject labels that sound like a campaign. Journey. Excellence. Community. Flourish. A parent comparing three schools will not open "Flourish" to find a fee. They will assume the site is performing, and they will return to a tab whose menu says "Fees."

Reject internal words. Advancement. Admissions office, if you can say "Visit" instead. Marketing. The family of schools, when you are one school. If a nickname is real on the playground and opaque on a first visit, teach it inside a page. Do not make it a top-level riddle.

Google's guidance on title links asks for descriptive titles that distinguish one page from another, not vague names and not the same boilerplate repeated on every URL. The menu deserves the same standard. The label and the page heading should describe the same destination. "Life" in the menu and "Our mission" on the page is a broken promise, however loyal the wording feels to the board.

Keep labels short enough to scan and specific enough to choose. Two words is often right. A sentence in the menu means the page never earned a name. Rewrite the page before you add a subtitle under the label.

## One path that visits or inquires

The visit is the action of the site. It gets a stable place: a text label in the header that says "Visit," visible on the first screen, on every page. If the next step for many families is an inquiry rather than an immediate tour, the label can say "Visit or inquire," as long as the page splits those two paths in the first screen. Do not hide the path under "Admissions" if "Admissions" opens a history of the school and a PDF.

The path should open dates or a short inquiry, not a film and not a crest. If open mornings are listed, the label should land on the list. A parent who taps "Visit" and meets a manifesto has been misdirected. Carry the child's likely age if the link can do it. At minimum, land them where a year group can be chosen without a speech.

Repeat the path at the end of long pages, in the same words. Header and closing link should match. "Visit" at the top and "Start your family's story" at the bottom are two products. Keep one verb.

Do not give equal weight to a second campaign. A fundraiser and a shop can exist. They do not sit in the same visual rank as the visit, or the menu has two missions and the parent has one. The eye should hit the visit without hunting. Rank is a kindness.

## What department names do

Department names comfort the org chart. Advancement. Academic board. Operations. They are meaningful on an internal slide. On the site they force a parent to guess which department holds the pickup time. Guessing is a tax. The other school is not charging it.

If you run a genuine second offer, such as a nursery with its own door and its own fee, give it a label the buyer uses. "Nursery" beats "Early years provision," and the page should state the ages and the separate visit. If the nursery closed, remove the label in the same week. Dead labels teach people that the menu is fiction.

A parents' association that wants a presence can have a footer link. It should not outrank fees. Current parents and prospective parents are different jobs. Mixing them in one header produces a menu that serves the louder committee and confuses the new family. You can serve current parents with a short, obvious link. You do not need to give them the whole bar.

Staff lists organized by department belong in the handbook. The public about page can name adults by what they do in the day, which is a job a parent understands. Navigation and that page should share nouns, or the school feels like two institutions.

## How deep the menu should be

One level is the goal for a school a parent can understand in a visit. Ages can open a short list if each age has a page that shows a different day. Visit should not have a submenu of slogans. Fees should not have a child link for every incidental charge if the pricing page already shows the shape. Depth is where parents get lost and where you forget a stale date.

If you need a second level, the parent item should be a real page, not a hover that some people never see. Phones do not hover. Keyboards should not have to discover a secret. WCAG's operable principle is the practical rule: a tap lands somewhere useful, and the same links exist without a mouse.

Dropdowns full of every news post are a drawer of old term dates. If you publish news, one label can point at the list. Individual posts do not belong in the header. They change, and the header should stay stable enough that a returning parent still knows where "Visit" is.

Five to seven labels, including the visit. When someone wants an eighth, remove one. Menus grow because each department asks. They shrink because a child is waiting on a decision and the parent is tired.

## Footer, header, and where you are

The header is for jobs. The footer is for the long tail: policies, a phone number, the postal door, privacy, a way to the question form. Do not invert this because a template put the pretty links at the bottom. A parent who needs fees will not enjoy finding them between charity numbers.

Mark the current page. A menu that does not show where you are forces people to reconstruct their place from headings alone. With three schools open, that is how someone reads the wrong fee and thinks you changed it.

The logo can go home. Home should then show students and a way to visit, or the logo is a loop back into a ceremony. Do not make the crest the only way to reach the visit. A path that depends on knowing your ritual is a puzzle.

If a document opens in a PDF, the label should say it is a document, or the parent thinks your site broke. Prefer a page. Use the PDF only when a third party demands the file, and make the HTML list enough for the decision.

## After they can find the day

Once the labels point at real jobs, the pages have to show students, or the menu is a promise with a crest behind it. Photography is the next decision, and schools get it wrong in a ceremonial way. [Which pictures belong on the site, and why a mission line is not a picture](/blog/photography-direction-for-an-independent-school) is the piece to read next. The menu can say "The day." The frame still has to contain a child who goes to this school.

If you want to walk the labels against the jobs parents actually bring, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current menu and the five questions the office hears most. The gaps between them are the redesign.
